title: Structural patterns: Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Proxy
description: How objects are composed: wrap, forward, tree-build and simplify, and how to tell Adapter, Decorator and Proxy apart.

questions.text: What do structural patterns deal with?

options.text: How classes and objects are composed into larger structures
How objects communicate at runtime only

questions.explanation: Structural patterns arrange classes and objects (wrapping, nesting, delegating) to build larger structures while keeping them flexible.

questions.text: Your code expects `PaymentGateway.charge()`, but a vendor SDK exposes `makePayment()` with different arguments. Which pattern fits?
questions.explanation: Adapter wraps the incompatible interface and translates calls to the one your code expects, without changing either side.

questions.text: Which pattern adds behaviour (compression, then encryption) to an object at runtime by wrapping it, keeping the same interface?
questions.explanation: Decorators wrap a component with the same interface and add behaviour before or after delegating. They can be stacked in any order.

questions.text: Which difference between Decorator and Proxy is the most useful?

options.text: None, they are the same class
Decorator adds behaviour the client chose; Proxy controls access to the same object (lazy load, cache, permission check)
Proxy changes the interface; Decorator keeps it

questions.explanation: Both keep the interface and hold a reference. A decorator is about extending behaviour; a proxy is about controlling access or cost: remote, virtual (lazy), protection, caching.

questions.text: A file explorer shows folders that contain files and other folders, and both respond to `size()`. Which pattern models this?
questions.explanation: Composite lets a client treat a single leaf and a group of children uniformly through one interface, which fits tree structures.

options.text: Gives a simple entry point to a complicated subsystem, which stays reachable for those who need it
Replaces an interface with an incompatible one

questions.explanation: A facade offers a small, task-oriented API over many classes. It does not hide the subsystem so strongly that nobody else may use it.

options.text: An abstraction from its implementation so that both can vary independently

questions.explanation: Bridge avoids a class explosion (for example Shape x Renderer = every combination as a subclass) by composing a Shape with a Renderer chosen separately.

questions.text: Flyweight saves memory by sharing the intrinsic (unchanging) part of many similar objects instead of storing a copy in each.
questions.explanation: True. Shared, immutable intrinsic state (such as a glyph shape) lives once; the extrinsic state (position) is passed in by the caller.

questions.text: Which of these are proxy use cases?

options.text: Loading a large image only when it is first displayed
Checking permissions before forwarding a call
Caching the result of a slow remote call

questions.explanation: Virtual (lazy), protection and caching proxies all control access to a real object. Translating an interface is the job of an Adapter.

questions.text: A logging wrapper and a retry wrapper both implement `HttpClient` and wrap another `HttpClient`. Which pattern is this, most likely?
questions.explanation: Each wrapper adds one behaviour while keeping the interface, so they can be stacked: retry(log(real)). Middleware pipelines follow the same idea.
